It's Titus Groan by Mervyn Peake. Rottcodd is a character in the book.

It's actually a part of a trilogy - the Gormenghast Trilogy. The other two books are Gormenghast and Titus Alone. I'd suggest reading both Titus Groan and Gormenghast, but Titus Alone is sort of optional. The first two tell a complete story and the third is a sort of odd and hasty sequel.

It's... it takes place in an enormous, sprawling, fictional castle named Gormenghast, and follows some of the most vividly bizarre characters ever conceived. Hi there, I’m CarlTheLlama, one of HotS' top support mains.

I'd like to talk about lane setups today, a subject I haven't seen brought up anywhere, and a problem I run into in some of the lower MMR games. In my experience of over 3k games, 2-1-2 is never an optimal setup. It simply doesn't have enough pressure to take advantages if you make plays and start doing well, and it doesn't interact favorably with the other lane setups (e.g. against double roaming it's always outnumbered when the gank squad shows up, so anyone trying to pressure gets punished for it). So what are your better options?

1-1-3:

The Tri-lane setup is probably most standard, it allows you to have a definite strong point, so you know where to pressure. It's easy to get some push down on turrets when you're gradually asserting your dominance, or grabbing a quick merc camp when you suddenly get a window after a favorable engage. The Tri-lane also optimizes support picks because supports' usefulness scales with the number of champions they are around to support.

Having strong solo laners is important to this kind of setup because there isn't going to be much roaming, so sustain is essential, as well as having an escape if the enemy team is running a gank squad. The nice thing about the tri-lane is it’s pretty reliable. Even if a gank squad shows up, it turns into a 3v3 where your tri-lane is on equal footing unless you go tower diving or you've just used a lot of cooldowns for little return. A tri-lane is a low-risk, moderate reward setup that also lets you move to objectives as (at least) a partial group quickly, and together which is often the most important factor to success in SoloQ.

In other words, the tri-lane is your go-to setup, it’s reliably good. That said, you can sometimes make some cool adaptations.

1-1-1 (2 roam):

It's often nice to have a champion like Kerrigan or Zeratul who is an assassin in the true sense of the word- they jump on you and say "Surprise, you're dead!" being able to have an extra element of surprise by coming out of the fog of war, and being able to pick the most extended/squishiest/least escapable/lowest health champions on the map means that these types of champions are best suited for roaming instead of staying in a lane.

Having weak laners who get pushed in is okay with this type of setup, since enemies pushing means they are more vulnerable to ganks. The most common way to mess up your roam comp is wave clear. While a Kerrigan combo may be able to clear a wave, staying missing will increase the success rate of the next gank. The whole point of early ganks however is to gain an advantage in soak, by either getting a kill and pushing the wave into tower quickly, or making them back and pushing the wave into tower. To do this, some follow-up waveclear after a gank is necessary. There are no hard and fast rules about how much/little to push, just remember your goals are to stay hidden as long as possible and deny experience when you're able to, and critically evaluate the situations as they come along to decided when/how much to clear to meet those goals.

1-1-1(2 stack)/1-2-1(1stack):

This is a niche setup, and is really only doable on maps with lanes close together: Dragon Shire, Tomb of the Spider Queen, and Blackhearts. On these maps however, champions like Raynor, Azmodan, and Tassadar can gain some surprising value from their ability to double stack their abilities. Getting Globes from each wave is essential, whether you're stacking Conjurer's pursuit or not, because the extra health and mana allows you to clear waves faster/more sustainably. The other important thing is to not spend time, cooldowns, or mana trading damage with the other team, simply clear the wave quickly for stacks, and move to the next lane for more.

You'll find that mid-lane waves meet a little before the other waves, so if you start there, clear quickly, move to the next lane, do the same,, then repeat, you quickly establish a rhythm where you get mass stacks, and simultaneously keep your opponent busy clearing waves instead of fighting you, negating some early game weaknesses inherent to having those stacking champions on your team.

I'd be careful of doing a triple-stacking comp, partly because it's good to keep the other team distracted with one person in the lane so they are less likely to set up an ambush on your stackers, and if they try you have someone to see it and warn you, but also because having more than 2 champions that are dependent on stacking is going to make your early game weak enough that you'll be bullied too much when trying to clear waves.
